SearchSearchFacebookTwitterEmailSMSBlue SkyWhatsappPrintRedditFlipboardPinterestLinkedinLatest StoriesPoliticsU.S. NewsWorldSportsBusinessHealthSelectedTiplineArtificial intelligenceAlphabet shares record their worst day ever, shedding $500 billion in valueThe sharp drop is the latest sign of anxiety creeping through Wall Street over how long it will take AI companies to see returns on massive investments.Listen to this article with a free profile00:0000:00Part of the reason Google's ad revenues from search underperformed is Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which results in fewer ads, a top executive told investors.David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via GettyShareAdd NBC News to GoogleOct. 29, 2026, 11:06 AM EDT / Updated Oct. 29, 2026, 4:33 PM EDTBy Steve KopackShares of Google parent company Alphabet sank Thursday by 12.6%, marking the stock’s worst one-day drop ever and wiping out $500 billion in market value.
Alphabet is America’s fourth-largest company, worth $3.47 trillion.
The market value it shed in Thursday’s trading session ranks as the second-worst one-day wipeout in U.S. market history, trailing only Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in late January 2025.
It was also the latest sign of broader anxiety across Wall Street over how long it will take big artificial intelligence companies to see consistent returns on investments worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
Late Thursday afternoon, Amazon’s stock appeared to be on track to meet a similar fate. The company reported third-quarter revenue after the bell that fell short of Wall Street’s expectations. Its shares quickly slid by 10% in after-hours trading.
Alphabet had reported its latest quarterly financial results Wednesday, revealing that revenues were less than had been anticipated and surprising investors.

A senior Alphabet executive told investors Wednesday that part of the reason ad revenues from search were underperforming was Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which was resulting in fewer ads.
The company is working on addressing that, Senior Vice President Philipp Schindler said on the investor call, adding that “ad experiments” in the feature have “shown promising results.”
Company executives tried to soften the blow for investors by touting more than 1 billion users of its Gemini AI app.

The company said in its July earnings report that it planned to spend more than $200 billion this year, double what it spent in 2025. It also raised almost $80 billion in capital in June, also to spend on the ever-expanding AI build-out.
Alphabet’s disappointing results also came against the backdrop of better results from its peer Microsoft, whose shares initially rose in after-hours trading Wednesday before they reversed course to end the day Thursday effectively flat.
The big drop in Alphabet shares dragged down the Nasdaq Composite index, which closed down 1.38%. The S&P 500 fell slightly less, by about 0.3%.
Shares of chip companies that supply equipment for AI data centers followed Alphabet shares lower, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropping 1.4%.
The bleeding even spread beyond the tech sector, as shares of the construction equipment giant Caterpillar — a key supplier of the machines required to build data centers — plunged 9.2% on Thursday.
Caterpillar’s recent earnings report revealed that its revenue beat Wall Street expectations but by less than many traders had hoped.
The sharp drop in its share price that followed made the industrial giant the day’s second-worst-performing stock in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, behind only Alphabet. The Dow declined slightly more than 130 points for the day.
As investors clamor for ever-higher returns from companies linked to the costly AI build-out, stock in firms that only narrowly top earnings targets, as Caterpillar did, has been getting punished in dramatic sell-offs.
